new_statements.rule_in_words: Each lexical word carries exactly one primary prominence (Carter: one underlying high tone H; Holder: the 'accent principal' H*), which is realised as high pitch on the stressed syllable. Its position is fixed per word and lexically distinctive (turkéy 'bird' vs Túrkey; practice vs practice; baker vs Bàkèr), with no dominant positional pattern: many words keep the English position, many others place the prominence one or two syllables further right (storý, jackét, watér, hospítal, coconút, organíze). Holder 1999 (pp. 62-64) gives the metrical generalisation: feet are unary or left-headed binary (trochaic), and the word accent plus its H tone goes to the head of the RIGHTMOST foot ('à gauche au niveau du pied, mais à droite au niveau du mot': kìndergárten, àllìgátor, càterpíllar, òrchéstra, hùrricáne, càlabásh), with foot parsing and extrametrical syllables lexically fixed (Ja(pán), (Cána)da, A(méri)ca). Both analyses call the system tonal / pitch accent-like rather than plain stress (Carter: ditonemic H/L; Holder: H* 'accent 1' vs B*H 'accent 2').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Carter: none in the tonal analysis — one underlying H per word/tone-group, all other syllables L (surface h by progressive assimilation before another tone group). Holder 1999: foot-level (N1) accents on the heads of non-final trochaic feet, i.e. secondary accents at two-syllable intervals (onomàtopéia, Dèmerára, kìndergárten), which carry no tone of their own.
new_statements.exceptions: (1) 'Accent 2' words (Holder pp. 64, 73-76 word list; Allsopp 1972; Devonish 1989): a lexically marked, mostly disyllabic set (sóda, táble, móney, hóspital, bícycle, ófficer, guava, hammock, Phagwah, Bàkèr as a surname) with LOW tone on the stressed syllable and HIGH on the following unstressed one; Carter transcribes the same words with H on the second syllable (sodá, watér, tabĺe, pensĺ). (2) Learned Greco-Latin words promote the penultimate foot instead of the rightmost (ózòne, ánecdòte, péntagòn, hypótenùse) (Holder p. 64). (3) Compounds: Carter — first member loses its H, second member gets H on its first syllable (English-péople, ballot-pápers, sea-wáter, fishermán; personal names keep the surname pattern: Paul-Nelsń); Holder — compounds follow the simple-word pattern with the main accent on the rightmost member and accent 2 effaced (kìtchen-táble, dìning-tàble, tàble-mát). (4) Iteration (táll ! táll 'very tall') keeps each word's pattern in separate tone groups; reduplication (tall-táll 'rather tall') behaves as a compound.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level in isolate citation forms, and the 'tone group' (Carter) / 'groupe accentuel' (Holder), which contains exactly one tonal accent: a simple word, a compound, or a lexical word plus its clitics (function words are unaccented and toneless; emphatic monosyllables like this, all, can't, when attract accent). Higher-level intonation (downdrift/downstep, final contours L%, H%, ↑H%) is described separately (Carter §2.4.1, Holder §§3.10-3.13).
new_statements.identity_note: Both opened primary sources describe the Guyanese English-lexicon creole continuum in its mesolectal/acrolectal range rather than the basilect: Carter 1987 calls her object 'Guyanese \"English-based\" Creole, or \"Creolese\"' but her data are Dennis Craig's recorded conference speech and Maurice Holder's word lists (English-vocabulary items such as accounts, hospital, organize); Holder 1999 labels the variety 'anglais est-caribéen'/'anglo-guyanais' with Guyana as the representative dialect and explicitly extends the same accentual system to Trinidad and Barbados, contrasting it with Jamaican. Glottolog has no separate code for acrolectal Guyanese English, so the key stays creo1235; the basilectal Creolese tone system proper is in Devonish 1989/2002 (not opened). APiCS (Devonish & Thompson) codes Creolese as a 'reduced tone system'.

sources.note: Section 2 (pp. 257-267) describes Guyanese as a two-tone (H/L) system built on stress: 'any syllable with primary stress has surface high pitch' (p. 258); every noun/verb/adjective/adverb has exactly one underlying H, 'no preference for certain patterns over others', and H often sits one or two syllables to the right of the English stress (storý, jackét, watér, hospítal, coconút, organíze) (pp. 264-266); compounds delete H on the first member and put H on the first syllable of the second (English-péople, ballot-pápers); lexical minimal pairs turkéy/Túrkey, gyal-frén/gyál!frén (p. 263); note 8…

sources.note: Whole article is on word accent of Eastern Caribbean English with Guyana as the representative variety (author a native speaker): main accent (accent 1) = high tone H* on a strong syllable; a lexically marked class (accent 2, B*H: sóda, táble, móney, hóspital, bícycle, ófficer) has low tone on the accented syllable and high on the next; accents are lexically distinctive (practice vs practice, baker vs Bàkèr) (p. 57, 64). Metrical rule: feet are unary or binary left-headed (trochees); 'la direction du gouvernement des constituants métriques est à gauche au niveau du pied, mais à droite au nive…
